name: Envato Market
tagline: Marketplace for buying WordPress themes, code, graphics, audio and video templates as one-off licensed purchases.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Envato Market items are priced individually rather than by subscription.

verdictSummary: Yes, the site is a listing grid with search, filters and a checkout. That part is a weekend, maybe less. The thing you cannot generate is a couple million licensed items from hundreds of thousands of authors, each with a rights agreement, a payout pipeline, reviews, refunds and version updates that keep working after WordPress ships a breaking release. A personal replacement has an empty catalog, and an empty marketplace is a database with a search box. The closest honest build is not a store at all: it is a local library for the licenses and files you already bought, which Envato's own downloads page handles badly enough that a replacement is genuinely useful.
coreLoopDIY: Indexes the theme, plugin and asset ZIPs you already purchased into a local searchable library with license keys, purchase codes, version notes and an update reminder per item.
requirements: Node 20 and a local folder of already purchased asset files
Your own purchase records exported or copied by hand
whatYouLose: The catalog itself: hundreds of thousands of items you did not make and cannot license
Author support, item updates and changelogs when a platform version breaks something
Ratings, sales counts and comment threads that tell you whether an item is abandoned
Legal cover: Envato's license agreement is the paper trail clients and auditors accept
Payment, tax handling and refunds for anything you might want to sell yourself
moatNotes: Two-sided and lopsided: buyers come for selection, authors come for buyers, and the license text is what makes commercial use defensible.
whyPeopleStillPay: People do not pay Envato for software, they pay for a specific item plus a license that lets them ship it to a paying client. The one-off price is usually a rounding error against the hours it replaces, and the license agreement is the part a client's lawyer will accept without a conversation. Even people who could build the same thing buy the theme because the value is the fifteen years of authors uploading, not the storefront wrapped around them.
notes: The storefront is a weekend; the catalog is not. The moat is marketplace liquidity plus a license agreement that clients accept without argument.
prompt:
Build a local single-user web app called "Asset Vault": a library for digital assets I have already purchased (themes, plugins, stock graphics, audio, video templates).

Stack, no substitutions: Node 20, TypeScript, Express, better-sqlite3, server-rendered EJS templates, Tailwind via CDN. No React, no build step beyond tsc. Runs with `npm install && npm run dev` on localhost:3000.

Data model in SQLite:
- item: id, name, author, kind (theme|plugin|graphic|audio|video|other), source (where bought), purchase_date, price_paid, currency, license_type, purchase_code, installed_version, latest_known_version, notes, archived (bool)
- file: id, item_id, path, filename, size_bytes, sha256, added_at
- tag and item_tag join table

Features, all local:
1. Point the app at one or more local folders via ASSET_ROOTS in .env. A scan command walks them, finds archives (zip, rar, 7z) and media files, hashes them, and creates one item per top-level archive with the filename as a guessed name. Re-scanning is idempotent by sha256.
2. Library view: card grid with search across name, author, tags and notes, plus filters for kind, source, license_type and archived.
3. Item detail page: edit every field inline, attach or detach files, copy purchase code to clipboard, open the containing folder path as text I can copy.
4. Bulk tag and bulk archive from the library view via checkboxes.
5. "Check for updates" is manual only: a field for latest_known_version and a flag on the library card when installed_version differs. Do not scrape or call any external site.
6. CSV import for purchase history (columns: name, author, purchase_date, price_paid, currency, license_type, purchase_code) matched to existing items by fuzzy name, with a preview screen before commit.
7. CSV and JSON export of everything.

Explicitly out of scope: user accounts, cloud sync, telemetry, any marketplace API, buying or selling, payments, license validation against a remote server.

Secrets and config in .env only (ASSET_ROOTS, PORT). Ship a README with the scan command, a seed script that creates three fake items, and vitest tests for the scanner's idempotency and the CSV importer's matching.
